implementation_notes: Scala's Boolean is a value type over the JVM primitive: if/while conditions require it, there is no truthiness and no numeric conversion, so the pattern's invariant already holds. Domain types expose predicates (`isEmpty`, `isDefined`, `nonEmpty`) and flags can be made nominal with an opaque type (Scala 3) or a value class so two Booleans are not interchangeable. Do not add a `given Conversion[MyType, Boolean]`: it would make `if (myValue)` compile again and put the object into every boolean context - exactly the accidental conversion the pattern removes.
code_sketch:
final case class Queue(size: Int):
  def isEmpty: Boolean = size == 0

if queue.isEmpty then println("empty")
// if queue then ...      // compile error: found Queue, required Boolean

opaque type IsEmpty = Boolean
object IsEmpty:
  def apply(b: Boolean): IsEmpty = b
  extension (e: IsEmpty) def value: Boolean = e
pitfalls: A `given Conversion[X, Boolean]` (or a Scala 2 implicit def) in scope reintroduces implicit testability and participates in overload resolution; keep boolean conversions out of scope.
Java interop brings the nullable java.lang.Boolean and boxed collections (java.util.List[java.lang.Boolean]); unboxing a null throws.
Opaque types erase to their underlying type at runtime, so an IsEmpty/IsValid distinction is compile-time only and disappears in Java-facing signatures.
